explain.say: Red means stop, green means go. But who decided that? The story starts on the railways! Look at the first point on the timeline. In the 1830s and 1840s, railways used coloured signals, and red, the colour of danger, could be seen from far away.

explain.say: Now see the fire at 1868. Outside the Houses of Parliament in London, horses and carts made the roads dangerous, so a railway engineer, John Peake Knight, built the first road signal. It had arms by day and red and green gas lamps at night, worked by a police officer.

explain.say: Great thinking! Look at the last point: timers and sensors took over, so nobody had to flip switches. Wow: the inventor Garrett Morgan patented a three-position signal in 1923, after seeing a crash. Today, some lights even turn green early for buses and ambulances!

faq.a: Red was already the colour of danger, and railways used it for stop signals because red light can be seen from a long way off.
asks: Why are traffic lights red, amber and green?

faq.q: What was the first traffic light?
faq.a: A gas-lit signal outside the Houses of Parliament in London, switched on in December 1868. It was designed by railway engineer John Peake Knight and worked by a police officer.
Detroit police officer William Potts made a three-colour, four-way signal in 1920, adding amber to warn that the light was changing.
asks: Who made the first three-colour traffic light?

faq.a: An African American inventor who patented a three-position traffic signal in 1923, after seeing a crash at a junction. He also invented a breathing hood used by firefighters.
asks: Did Garrett Morgan invent the traffic light?

faq.q: How do traffic lights know when to change?
faq.a: Some run on timers, while others use sensors in the road or cameras to spot waiting cars and people, and a computer controls the sequence.

facts: The first road traffic signal was installed outside the Houses of Parliament in London on 10 December 1868.
In 1920, Detroit police officer William Potts created a three-colour traffic light.
